analysis.one_liner: Toughens FDA oversight of drug makers and importers with mandatory recalls, higher fines, and whistleblower protections.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 17, 2010, less than three weeks before the 111th Congress expired, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required drug manufacturers — in the U.S. and abroad — to register with the FDA, run real quality-control systems, and open their plants to regular inspections, with foreign plants held to the same standard as domestic ones. It would have given the FDA power to order recalls of contaminated drugs, detain or destroy dangerous imports, and impose fines up to $500,000 per violation and prison terms up to 10 years for knowing violations, while protecting employees who blow the whistle on safety problems. It was introduced in the final weeks of a Congress that was about to expire and died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who takes prescription drugs. The bill targets the ways unsafe medicine reaches people: contaminated ingredients, counterfeit or adulterated products, plants that block inspectors, and companies that sit on recall decisions. It would have required manufacturers to trace their supply chains back to source materials, let the FDA order a recall instead of merely asking, ban imports without safety documentation, and protect the employees who report violations. People harmed by unsafe drugs, and their families, would also have gained new civil remedies, and whistleblowers would have gotten protection from retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: It requires every drug maker to run an 'effective quality system' covering supply-chain risk management, independent quality units, and accurate records, and makes drugs produced without one legally adulterated.

It requires FDA inspection of every drug plant at least once every two to four years, and puts foreign and domestic plants on equal footing — closing a gap that mattered as more drug ingredients were made abroad.

It gives FDA authority to order a stop to distribution and a mandatory recall of contaminated or misbranded drugs, plus power to detain and, for imports posing serious health risks, destroy dangerous shipments.

It raises the stakes for violations: civil penalties up to $500,000 per violation ($10 million per proceeding), criminal penalties of up to 10 years for knowing drug-safety violations, and forfeiture of profits from violations.
It expands whistleblower protections for employees who refuse to violate the law or report violations — the people best positioned to catch problems before patients are harmed.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers and importers. They would have paid new annual registration fees, built quality-system and supply-chain tracking programs, absorbed supplier audits and inspections, and faced civil penalties up to $500,000 per violation, criminal exposure up to 10 years, and forfeiture of profits for knowing safety violations. Some of those compliance costs could show up in drug prices.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers, importers, and customs brokers would bear new annual registration fees and the cost of building quality systems, supply-chain tracking, and supplier audit programs, and some of that cost could be passed on in drug prices.

Small manufacturers could find the fixed compliance overhead of an 'effective quality system' and full supply-chain documentation relatively heavier than large firms do, which could push marginal producers out of the market.

The bill greatly expands government coercive powers over the drug supply — administrative detention, destruction of imports sometimes with notice after the fact for low-value or hazardous goods, and civil and criminal asset forfeiture — which, whatever the safety rationale, concentrates significant discretion in the agency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to anyone who takes medicine: mandatory quality systems, equalized foreign inspections, mandatory recall authority, and 10-year criminal penalties target the kinds of failures — contaminated ingredients, counterfeit drugs, concealed defects — that have repeatedly harmed patients. The costs are real but narrower: manufacturers and importers pay registration fees and compliance costs, which could nudge drug prices up or squeeze the smallest producers, and the bill's new detention, seizure, and forfeiture powers deserve scrutiny to ensure they are applied with due process. On balance, a stronger safety net for the drug supply outweighs the compliance burden, and the bill's design — fees that fund the inspections, hardship waivers, appeal windows — acknowledges the cost side.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the closing days of a Congress that had only weeks left, got referred to committee, and expired there when the new Congress was seated — nobody ever voted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2010, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
It had a Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers and importers are better off: they never faced the new registration fees, mandatory quality systems and recalls, or the much larger civil and criminal penalties the bill would have imposed. Patients gained nothing from its death.

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 17, 2010 and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Reps. Henry Waxman, Frank Pallone, and Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no further action was taken on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only four House Democrats are on record — the sponsor and three cosponsors — with no Republican support and no recorded opponent, so no bloc ever took a position in the record; the bill simply ran out of time.

industries.note: The bill imposes annual registration fees, mandatory quality systems, supply-chain documentation, biennial inspections with equal treatment of foreign plants, and much larger civil and criminal penalties, including forfeiture of violation proceeds. These costs buy a safer drug supply for patients, so the industry's interest in avoiding them runs against the public's interest in safety — though reputable manufacturers also gain from a level playing field that punishes bad actors.

Importers would have to register with FDA, pay fees, follow 'good importer practices' to verify their sources, and face registration suspension for violations; customs brokers face new registration requirements. The compliance burden funds import safety review that protects consumers from adulterated or counterfeit drugs.

The bill funds FDA's drug safety work through industry fees and grants the agency new powers: mandatory recalls, administrative detention, destruction of dangerous imports, and subpoena authority. A stronger FDA is the public's enforcement arm, so this gain runs alongside the public's interest.
